passage.title: Moonlight on the Cumberland Dunes
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Elena clicked on her red flashlight as she followed Aunt Rosa across the wind-swept dunes of Cumberland Island. On this wild Georgia barrier island, loggerhead sea turtles crawled ashore every summer to bury their eggs in the warm sand. Tonight, Nest 14 was finally ready to hatch under a sky shrouded in thick coastal fog. Elena knew they had to use red light instead of white beams. That way, they would not startle the baby turtles. By nature's ancient instinct, newborn hatchlings always scramble toward the brightest low horizon. On most nights, that is the moonlit ocean surf.

When they reached the wire screen guarding Nest 14, dozens of tiny dark shells were already boiling up from the sand pit. Yet the hatchlings did not march down the wet slope toward the waves. Instead, they spun in confused circles. Emerging from the warm sand pit beneath the foggy sky, the tiny loggerhead hatchlings were strangely disoriented by a pale glow behind the sea oats. Nearly twenty of the babies began crawling uphill toward the dark woods. Aunt Rosa gasped and knelt to block their path with her canvas clipboard.

Aunt Rosa whispered that no houses or streetlamps stood within two miles of this north beach sector. Elena climbed to the top of the high dune. She scanned the dark tree line behind them. Through a gap in the live oaks, she spotted a bright white lantern on the stern of a shrimp boat in the back sound. Because thick fog covered the ocean to the east, that single boat lamp in the western marsh shone brighter than the sea.

Even worse, a puddle of rainwater in the low trough between the dunes acted like a mirror. It reflected the boat's white glare right into the eyes of the turtles at the nest. The hatchlings were being lured away from the surf by a trick of fog and water. Elena knew they could not reach the boat in time. The babies would dry out by dawn if they wandered into the woods.

Thinking fast, Elena unzipped her rain poncho and asked Aunt Rosa to hold the other two corners. Together, they stretched the dark nylon tarp along the top of the ridge like a wide curtain. As soon as the tarp blocked the boat's reflection, the dune trough fell dark again. Within seconds, the hatchlings pivoted in the sand, spotted the faint white foam of the ocean rollers, and paddled safely into the surf.

tier2Words.definition: covered or hidden from view as if wrapped in a thick cloth
tier2Words.rootHint: Old English 'scrud' (a garment or covering wrap)

tier2Words.definition: an inborn pattern of behavior that animals follow naturally without being taught
tier2Words.contextClue: Newborn hatchlings naturally scramble toward the brightest low horizon as soon as they hatch.

tier2Words.definition: having lost one's sense of direction and confused about which way to go
tier2Words.contextClue: Instead of marching toward the waves, the hatchlings spun in confused circles.

tier2Words.definition: drawn or tempted away toward something, often into danger
tier2Words.rootHint: Old French 'loirre' (a bait or decoy used to call hawks)
tier2Words.contextClue: The bright reflection drew the hatchlings uphill away from the safe surf.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Emerging from the warm sand pit beneath the foggy sky, the tiny loggerhead hatchlings were strangely disoriented by a pale glow behind the sea oats."

Based on the structure of this sentence, what caused the confusion?

options.text: A pale glow shining behind the sea oats
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'were strangely disoriented by a pale glow behind the sea oats' tells us that the pale glow behind the sea oats caused the hatchlings' confusion.

options.text: The warm sand pit beneath the wire screen
options.childFeedback: The warm sand pit is simply where the hatchlings emerged from; it did not confuse their sense of direction.

options.text: The tiny loggerhead hatchlings climbing the dune
options.childFeedback: The tiny loggerhead hatchlings are the ones who felt disoriented, not the thing that caused the confusion.

options.text: Elena's red flashlight beam on the beach
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 explains that Elena used a red flashlight specifically so the beam would not startle or confuse the baby turtles.

questions.provingSentenceText: Emerging from the warm sand pit beneath the foggy sky, the tiny loggerhead hatchlings were strangely disoriented by a pale glow behind the sea oats.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the phrase 'were strangely disoriented by a pale glow behind the sea oats' tells us that the pale glow behind the sea oats caused the hatchlings' confusion.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive construction, 'the tiny loggerhead hatchlings' receive the action of being disoriented. The true cause/actor follows the preposition 'by': 'a pale glow behind the sea oats' (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Look at the words right after 'disoriented by' in the Paragraph 2 sentence to see what confused the baby turtles.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"The hatchlings were being lured away from the surf by a trick of fog and water."

What does the word "lured" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: Protected from hungry birds by a wire screen
options.childFeedback: The wire screen guarded the nest in Paragraph 2, whereas in Paragraph 4 the hatchlings are being pulled away from the surf into danger.

options.text: Washed out to sea by a high wave
options.childFeedback: The turtles hadn't reached the ocean waves yet—they were crawling uphill away from the surf toward the reflection in the dune puddle.

options.text: Drawn or pulled toward something
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'lured' means drawn or pulled toward something, because the bright reflection in the rainwater puddle was tricking the baby turtles into crawling toward the woods.

options.text: Hidden permanently beneath the wet sand
options.childFeedback: The hatchlings had already boiled up out of the sand pit in Paragraph 2 and were crawling across the dunes, not hidden under the sand.

questions.provingSentenceText: The hatchlings were being lured away from the surf by a trick of fog and water.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'lured' means drawn or pulled toward something, because the bright reflection in the rainwater puddle was tricking the baby turtles into crawling toward the woods.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 4, the reflected glare of the boat lantern acts as a false beacon that pulls ('lured') the hatchlings uphill away from the ocean surf (Option C).
questions.retryHint: Think about how the reflected white glare in Paragraph 4 was pulling the hatchlings away from the ocean surf and toward the trees.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 3, why did the shrimp boat's lantern look brighter to the turtles than the ocean horizon?

options.text: The shrimp boat had sailed right onto the dry sand of the high dune near Nest 14.
options.childFeedback: The shrimp boat was floating in the water of the back sound behind the live oaks, not sitting on the dry sand of the high dune.

options.text: Thick fog covered the ocean to the east, making the single white lamp in the western marsh stand out more brightly.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that because thick fog covered the ocean to the east, the single white lantern on the shrimp boat in the western marsh shone brighter than the sea.

options.text: Aunt Rosa pointed her white flashlight beam at the live oak trees to see the forest path.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 explains that Elena and Aunt Rosa carefully used red light instead of white flashlight beams so they wouldn't confuse the turtles.

options.text: The moon never rises over the Atlantic Ocean during the summer hatching season.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 says that on most summer nights the moonlit ocean surf is the brightest horizon; tonight was different only because of the thick coastal fog.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because thick fog covered the ocean to the east, that single boat lamp in the western marsh shone brighter than the sea.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that because thick fog covered the ocean to the east, the single white lantern on the shrimp boat in the western marsh shone brighter than the sea.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 directly explains the environmental cause: 'Because thick fog covered the ocean to the east, that single boat lamp in the western marsh shone brighter than the sea' (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Read the last sentence of Paragraph 3 to see how the eastern fog affected the brightness of the ocean compared to the boat lamp.

questions.prompt: How do Paragraphs 2 through 5 work together to form the main structure of the story?

options.text: They explain why Cumberland Island should ban all visitors from walking on the beach at night.
options.childFeedback: The story never calls for banning visitors from Cumberland Island; in fact, Elena and Aunt Rosa's night patrol saves Nest 14.

options.text: They compare the diet of loggerhead sea turtles with the diet of fish living in the western marsh.
options.childFeedback: The passage focuses on guiding newborn hatchlings safely to the surf, never mentioning what adult turtles or marsh fish eat.

options.text: They present a sudden mystery when the hatchlings crawl the wrong way, uncover the hidden cause, and show Elena's quick solution.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 2 through 5 trace a clear problem-and-solution arc: the hatchlings crawl the wrong way (Paragraph 2), Elena spots the boat lamp and puddle reflection (Paragraphs 3–4), and her poncho blocks the glare (Paragraph 5).

options.text: They list the tools Aunt Rosa packed inside her canvas clipboard before leaving home.
options.childFeedback: Aunt Rosa only uses her canvas clipboard in Paragraph 2 to block the baby turtles' uphill path, not to unpack a list of tools.

questions.provingSentenceText: As soon as the tarp blocked the boat's reflection, the dune trough fell dark again.
questions.childTip: Paragraphs 2 through 5 trace a clear problem-and-solution arc: the hatchlings crawl the wrong way (Paragraph 2), Elena spots the boat lamp and puddle reflection (Paragraphs 3–4), and her poncho blocks the glare (Paragraph 5).
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RL5, Paragraphs 2–5 follow a classic problem-investigation-resolution narrative structure: Paragraph 2 introduces the disoriented hatchlings, Paragraphs 3–4 uncover the lantern and puddle reflection, and Paragraph 5 resolves the crisis with the poncho barrier (Option C).
questions.retryHint: Trace the sequence from the confused hatchlings in Paragraph 2, to what Elena spots in Paragraphs 3–4, to her poncho solution in Paragraph 5.

questions.prompt: PART A: Why did stretching Elena's dark rain poncho along the dune ridge immediately cause the hatchlings to turn toward the ocean?

options.text: By blocking the artificial glare from the marsh, the poncho allowed the faint natural glow of the ocean foam to become the brightest horizon again.
options.childFeedback: Because hatchlings instinctively crawl toward the brightest horizon (Paragraph 1), blocking the boat's reflection with the dark poncho let the faint white ocean foam become the brightest light again.

options.text: The loud flapping sound of the nylon poncho scared the hatchlings down the slope into the water.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 never says the poncho made a loud flapping sound to scare the turtles; it worked like a dark curtain that blocked the light.

options.text: The poncho acted like a giant slide that carried the baby turtles over the sea oats into the waves.
options.childFeedback: Elena and Aunt Rosa held the poncho upright along the ridge like a curtain to block the reflection, not flat on the ground like a slide.

options.text: The dark tarp made the coastal fog disappear completely from the sky above Cumberland Island.
options.childFeedback: Stretching a rain poncho along a sand dune only shaded the puddle trough—it could not make coastal fog vanish from the sky.

questions.provingSentenceText: Within seconds, the hatchlings pivoted in the sand, spotted the faint white foam of the ocean rollers, and paddled safely into the surf.
questions.childTip: Because hatchlings instinctively crawl toward the brightest horizon (Paragraph 1), blocking the boat's reflection with the dark poncho let the faint white ocean foam become the brightest light again.
questions.parentExplanation: Synthesizing Paragraph 1 (hatchlings instinctively head toward the brightest low horizon) with Paragraph 5 shows that once the poncho blocked the artificial boat reflection, the faint white foam of the ocean rollers became the brightest light source again (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Connect the turtle instinct described at the end of Paragraph 1 with what happened to the dune trough in Paragraph 5 once the poncho blocked the boat's glare.

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "On this wild Georgia barrier island, loggerhead sea turtles crawled ashore every summer to bury their eggs in the warm sand."
options.childFeedback: This background sentence from Paragraph 1 only tells when mother turtles lay eggs, not how Elena's poncho helped the hatchlings find the ocean.

options.text: "Aunt Rosa whispered that no houses or streetlamps stood within two miles of this north beach sector."
options.childFeedback: This line from Paragraph 3 only explains that there were no houses or streetlights nearby, before Elena even spotted the shrimp boat.

options.text: "Even worse, a puddle of rainwater in the low trough between the dunes acted like a mirror."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 4 describes the puddle problem that tricked the turtles, rather than showing how blocking the light solved it.

options.text: "Within seconds, the hatchlings pivoted in the sand, spotted the faint white foam of the ocean rollers, and paddled safely into the surf."
options.childFeedback: This quotation from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by showing the hatchlings turning around, spotting the faint white foam of the ocean rollers, and paddling into the surf.

questions.provingSentenceText: Within seconds, the hatchlings pivoted in the sand, spotted the faint white foam of the ocean rollers, and paddled safely into the surf.
questions.childTip: This quotation from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by showing the hatchlings turning around, spotting the faint white foam of the ocean rollers, and paddling into the surf.
questions.parentExplanation: Option D provides the exact verbatim proof from Paragraph 5 showing that once the false light was blocked, the hatchlings spotted the faint white foam of the ocean rollers and oriented toward the surf.
questions.retryHint: Find the quote from Paragraph 5 that shows what the hatchlings spotted and did right after the poncho blocked the boat's glare.
